evidence_quotes.quote: Using observations and in-depth interviews with small-scale sanitation service providers, this study investigated the constraints and motivations of sanitation-related businesses in peri-urban communities in the Ningo–Prampram district of Ghana.

evidence_quotes.page: PDF Page 3 (Methodology - Population, sampling and data collection)
evidence_quotes.quote: The study participants, comprising of three masons/latrine builders, two sanitation hardware suppliers, and a pit-emptier, were selected using non-probability sampling techniques based on purpose, convenience and availability of the participants.
In addition, the masons mentioned that it was not necessary for them to register their business because they operate as local masons and did not need any formal documents

previously, there were three dumping sites for fecal sludge but all have been sold to individuals for their private businesses, a situation which compels us to travel long distances at higher costs to dump fecal sludge

Notwithstanding the threat of the constraints, it was found that the small-scale sanitation service providers are making a healthy proﬁt margin, which serves to motivate them to stay and continue in their respective businesses.

criterion_notes.c1: No. Although situated in the peri-urban sanitation sector in Ghana, the study does not examine household or community sanitation service access; instead, it investigates entrepreneurship, operational business constraints, and financial profitability among six small-scale sanitation businesses (three masons/latrine builders, two hardware suppliers, and one pit-emptier).
criterion_notes.c2: No under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading (and only tangential/enterprise-level under the plain wording). Under the plain/literal broad wording of Criterion 2, the study briefly mentions institutional and administrative challenges facing small businesses—specifically business registration costs and bureaucracy at the Registrar General's Department (needed to bid on District Assembly projects), small-business taxation, unauthorized police stops on a septic truck, land litigation slowing building, and the sale of former fecal sludge dumping sites to private individuals. However, even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the overall paper would still be excluded because it studies vendor business constraints and profit margins rather than household or community service access (failing Criteria 1 and 4). Under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading, Criterion 2 is clearly not met: none of these enterprise-level business-environment complaints are analysed as a rule-type legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism directly governing household or community sanitation service access (such as eligibility screening, tenure/documentation rules, tariff/cost-recovery regulation, or enforcement governing user access).
criterion_notes.c3: Yes. Empirical mixed-methods multiple-case study based on primary field data collected in 2012-2013 via transect walks and structured/semi-structured in-depth interviews with six small-scale sanitation service providers, reporting constraint rankings and operating profit margin calculations.
criterion_notes.c4: No. Reported outcomes are ranked operational constraints on small-scale sanitation enterprises (Table 2) and enterprise operating profit margins of 27-46% motivating entrepreneurs to remain in business (Table 3). No household or community outcome of sanitation access, connection, coverage, reliability, quantity, affordability, or exclusion is measured.
criterion_notes.c5: Yes. The population and unit of analysis (six small-scale sanitation service providers/businesses in four peri-urban communities of Ningo-Prampram district), exposures (internal and external business constraints and financial/non-financial motivations), outcomes (ranked business constraints and enterprise profit margins), and study design (mixed-methods multiple-case study) are clearly identifiable, though defined at the small-enterprise profitability level rather than household/community service access.
criterion_notes.c6: Yes. Full text is written in English.

study_design: Mixed-methods descriptive and explanatory multiple-case study (transect walk observations and structured/semi-structured in-depth interviews)
population_and_sample: Six local small-scale sanitation service providers (SSPs) in four peri-urban communities (Olowey, Kley, Lower East Prampram, and Lower West Prampram) in the Ningo-Prampram district, Greater Accra region, Ghana: three masons/latrine builders, two sanitation hardware suppliers, and one pit-emptier (convenience/purposive sample)
exposure: Internal and external factors constraining or motivating small-scale sanitation business operations (primarily client credit/delayed payment, lack of capital, hardware cost/quality, and dumping-site distance, alongside enterprise registration, small-business taxes, land litigation, and police stops)
outcome: Ranked constraints to small-scale sanitation business operations and enterprise operating profit margins (27% to 46%) motivating service providers to remain in business
rationale: Excluded at full text (E04: Wrong outcome; also fails Criteria 1 and 2). This mixed-methods multiple-case study interviews six small-scale sanitation entrepreneurs (three masons, two hardware suppliers, and one pit-emptier) in peri-urban Ningo-Prampram, Ghana, to rank their business challenges and estimate enterprise operating profit margins (27-46%). It does not measure or report any household or community sanitation access, connection, availability, reliability, quantity, affordability, or exclusion outcome (c4=no; c1=no). Moreover, under the 2026-10-13 narrow reading of Criterion 2, it does not examine a rule-type legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism directly governing household/community service access, mentioning only enterprise-level business environment issues (business registration for District Assembly contracts, small-business taxes, police stops, and sale of dumping sites) among broader market/financial challenges (c2=no). Even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the study remains excluded because its unit of analysis and outcomes concern small-enterprise profitability rather than household or community sanitation service access.
